neighbours.label: best guess: stating what category something formally / technically counts as ('is technically a fruit'): fires on ' technically' and the category noun
fire: A peanut is technically a legume, even though everyone calls it a nut.
The island is technically part of France, although it lies in the Caribbean.
A whale is technically a mammal, despite living its whole life at sea.
The shed is technically a dwelling under the planning rules, since it has a bed.
Pluto is technically a dwarf planet according to the 2006 definition.
The scooter is technically a motor vehicle, so you need insurance to ride it.
A strawberry is technically not a berry at all in the botanical sense.
The contract is technically still valid, because nobody ever cancelled it.
quiet: A peanut is a cheap snack, and nearly everyone in the office likes them.
The island is a long way from France, since it lies in the Caribbean.
A whale surfaced beside the boat and spent the whole afternoon near us.
The shed is full of old tools and paint tins, and it has a broken door.
Pluto was discovered in 1930 by a young astronomer working in Arizona.
The scooter is bright yellow, so you can see it from across the square.
A strawberry tastes best in June when the weather has been warm and dry.
The lawyer lost the papers, because nobody ever filed them properly.

notes: Card: ' technically' x4, then single cases (' quotient' rule, senior ' citizen', directional ' derivative', correct ' choice'); output promotes ' formal', ' formally', ' status'. Probes were weak: 'technically a fruit' 0.39 but 'a tasty fruit' 0.26 too; 'technically covered' 0.26; legal and maths terms 0.05-0.16. Near misses keep the sentence and drop the formal-classification framing; two of them may fire.
